title: Integrated Rate Laws
lead: Integrating a rate law gives an equation for how the concentration of a reactant changes with time. The section writes these integrated rate laws for first-, second-, and zero-order reactions, reads the order and the rate constant of a reaction from plots of its data, and defines the half-life of a reaction.
objectives: Explain the form and function of an integrated rate law
Perform integrated rate law calculations for zero-, first-, and second-order reactions
Define half-life and carry out related calculations
Identify the order of a reaction from concentration/time data
summary_html:
Integrated rate laws are mathematically derived from differential rate laws, and they describe the time dependence of reactant and product concentrations.

The half-life of a reaction is the time required to decrease the amount of a given reactant by one-half. A reaction’s half-life varies with rate constant and, for some reaction orders, reactant concentration. The half-life of a zero-order reaction decreases as the initial concentration of the reactant in the reaction decreases. The half-life of a first-order reaction is independent of concentration, and the half-life of a second-order reaction decreases as the concentration increases.

I-131 ⟶ Xe-131 + electron
The decay is first-order with a rate constant of 0.138 d−1. How many days will it take for 90% of the iodine−131 in a 0.500 M solution of this substance to decay to Xe-131?

answer.hint: Ninety percent decayed leaves 10%, so ln([A]0/[A]t) = ln 10; divide by k.

exercises.prompt: The zero-order plot in Figure 12.11 shows an initial ammonia concentration of 0.0028 mol L<sup>−1</sup> decreasing linearly with time for 1000 s. Assuming no change in this zero-order behavior, at what time (min) will the concentration reach 0.0001 mol L<sup>−1</sup>?

answer.hint: Solve [A]t = −kt + [A]0 for t with k = 1.3 × 10−6 mol L−1 s−1, then convert seconds to minutes.

exercises.prompt: The first-order radioactive decay of iodine-131 exhibits a rate constant of 0.138 d<sup>−1</sup>. What is the half-life for this decay?
What is the half-life (min) for the thermal decomposition of ammonia on tungsten (see Example 12.10)?

answer.hint: The reaction is zero order, so t1/2 = [A]0/2k with [A]0 = 0.0028 mol L−1 and k = 1.3 × 10−6 mol L−1 s−1.

exercises.prompt: Describe how graphical methods can be used to determine the order of a reaction and its rate constant from a series of data that includes the concentration of A at varying times.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: from the data, work out ln[A] and 1/[A] at each time, then plot [A], ln[A] and 1/[A] against time. Only one of the three plots is a straight line, and it names the order: [A] against t for a zero-order reaction, ln[A] against t for a first-order reaction, and 1/[A] against t for a second-order reaction. Read the slope of that line from two points near its ends; the rate constant is the negative of the slope for zero and first order and the slope itself for second order.

exercises.prompt: What is the half-life for the first-order decay of phosphorus-32? (<sup>32</sup><sub>15</sub>P ⟶ <sup>32</sup><sub>16</sub>S + e<sup>−</sup>) The rate constant for the decay is 4.85 × 10<sup>−2</sup> day<sup>−1</sup>.
What is the half-life for the decomposition of NOCl when the concentration of NOCl is 0.15 M? The rate constant for this second-order reaction is 8.0 × 10−8 L mol−1 s−1.

The reaction of compound A to give compounds C and D was found to be second-order in A. The rate constant for the reaction was determined to be 2.42 L mol−1 s−1. If the initial concentration is 0.500 mol/L, what is the value of t1/2?

Some bacteria are resistant to the antibiotic penicillin because they produce penicillinase, an enzyme with a molecular weight of 3 × 104 g/mol that converts penicillin into inactive molecules. Although the kinetics of enzyme-catalyzed reactions can be complex, at low concentrations this reaction can be described by a rate law that is first order in the catalyst (penicillinase) and that also involves the concentration of penicillin. From the following data: 1.0 L of a solution containing 0.15 µg (0.15 × 10−6 g) of penicillinase, determine the order of the reaction with respect to penicillin and the value of the rate constant.
[Penicillin] (M)Rate (mol L−1 min−1)
2.0 × 10−61.0 × 10−10
3.0 × 10−61.5 × 10−10
4.0 × 10−62.0 × 10−10

parts.hint: Compare how the rate changes as the penicillin concentration doubles.
The rate law is rate = k[penicillinase][penicillin]; find the molar concentration of penicillinase from its mass and molecular weight.

answer.solution: The reaction is first order. k = 1.0 × 107 L mol−1 min−1

exercises.prompt:
There are two molecules with the formula C3H6. Propene, CH3CH=CH2, is the monomer of the polymer polypropylene, which is used for indoor-outdoor carpets. Cyclopropane is used as an anesthetic:

When heated to 499 °C, cyclopropane rearranges (isomerizes) and forms propene with a rate constant of 5.95 × 10−4 s−1. What is the half-life of this reaction? What fraction of the cyclopropane remains after 0.75 h at 499 °C?

parts.hint: The reaction is first order, so t1/2 = 0.693/k.
Convert 0.75 h to seconds and use [A]t/[A]0 = e−kt.

exercises.prompt: Suppose that the half-life of steroids taken by an athlete is 42 days. Assuming that the steroids biodegrade by a first-order process, how long would it take for 1/64 of the initial dose to remain in the athlete’s body?

answer.hint: One sixty-fourth is one-half multiplied by itself six times.
